summary:
Osun operates inside Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country, in Osun State as in every other state, and reaches visitors and non-citizens as well as residents. Human Rights Watch (October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe') records that the statute bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

The statute binds people beyond the couple. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026 states that the law also reaches those who arrange or organise same-sex weddings and anyone involved with gay groups. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

A parallel religious criminal law layer in twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. That layer does not extend to Osun, which sits outside the Sharia states, and the FCDO death-penalty warning is expressly confined to northern states. The federal penalties and the arrest-risk warnings apply in full.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is current and blunt. The FCDO advisory of 19 August 2026 warns travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and states that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Enforcement rests on appearance and suspicion as much as on evidence. In March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the Act as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. Human Rights Watch has documented police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under the statute.

Trans visitors face lethal violence, official misgendering and impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in Abuja in August 2024, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. In February 2025, six months on, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Enforcement also takes the form of mass arrests at social venues, a national pattern rather than a local one. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011; more than 100 party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda in Lagos in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri in August 2023; and 76 people at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. Foreign and domestic guidance should be read against that record when a visitor considers attending any private gathering.
tangentialFactors:
Discrete criminalisation of presentation has been proposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing; whether such a proposal has advanced into law is not resolved by the available sourcing, but the drafting itself signals the direction of legislative attention on gender presentation.

A decade-outcome assessment of the statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the Act, finds that the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

The constitutional text points the other way. The BBC report of 9 August 2024 notes that Nigeria guarantees non-discrimination and private and family life in its constitution, while mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. The gap between guarantee and enforcement is the operative condition, and it holds in the south as well, where the Lagos and Delta State arrests took place.

Enforcement intensity is uneven by geography. The heaviest penalties and the death-penalty exposure sit in the twelve northern states under Sharia; the southern states operate under the federal statute alone, with arrests still recorded at social venues and on the street. Osun falls in the second group, which reduces the exposure relative to the north without changing the 10 to 14 year federal range.
localsOnly:
Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work. Residents who depend on local services bear that constriction continuously rather than during a visit.

Imprisonment of a prominent transgender woman raised placement questions with a documented finding behind them. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure and exposure of their members. The House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008, and some of those named were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Employment and public life carry documented costs since 2014: LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and increased attacks, and the ten-year assessment finds the statute has effectively sanctioned abuse well beyond its stated scope.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Osun-specific enforcement record is sourced. The inventory contains no prosecutions, police directives, venue closures or state-command instructions attributable to Osun State itself; the documented arrests, killings and detentions are located in other states and in the federal capital, and are carried here as evidence of the national framework Osun stands under.

The status of the cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters in September 2022 is unresolved. Whether they were introduced as bill, enacted, or abandoned is not stated in the available sourcing.

The investigation into the killing of 'Abuja Area Mama' is unresolved beyond February 2025. The Dial's report of that month records that no suspects had been charged; no later outcome is sourced, and no finding on motive or on the police characterisation of the victim is available.

Whether the placement practice identified by the October 2024 panel was corrected after the finding that maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act is not sourced.

No data is available on trans-specific facilities, shelters, identity-document marker rules or healthcare access within Osun State, and none should be inferred from the national material above.
